 Advertisement Northern California elections officials say how they would handle Election Day threats, other issues
 Six elections officials we interviewed described ways to report election concerns, accommodate voters already in line when polls close, and respond to interference or threats. Here is how they would respond to eight scenarios. 
 Advertisement Updated: 7:06 PM PDT Oct 31, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Lee Anne Denyer Reporter Northern California elections officials say how they would handle Election Day threats, other issues
 Six elections officials we interviewed described ways to report election concerns, accommodate voters already in line when polls close, and respond to interference or threats. Here is how they would respond to eight scenarios. 
 Updated: 7:06 PM PDT Oct 31, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Lee Anne Denyer Reporter KCRA 3 connected with voter registrars in Northern California to better understand how they would respond to various problems that may arise on Nov. 3, Election Day. 
 All six elections officials interviewed on Friday described ways to report election concerns, accommodate voters already in line when polls close, and respond to interference or threats. 
 Advertisement How to track your ballot in California for the Nov. 3 midterm election The clearest differences were in the specific backup systems, complaint channels and ballot-tracking procedures each official described. 
 See below for how they would react to eight scenarios. 
 Q: How are backup ballots delivered, and what should voters do if supplies run low? 
 Officials said they prepare extra ballot supplies and have backup options. A location running low would generally contact the elections office, which could send more supplies through field staff. Some counties, including Sutter County, also described printing ballots on demand or using emergency ballots.
 “We have the ICX touch units and those have what we call a full-face ballot, so we can print blank ballots from those on demand,” said Donna Johnston, Sutter County Clerk-Recorder/Registrar of Voters.
 In San Joaquin County, the registrar of voters said ballot printing can be done at sites as needed. 
 “We are a traditional polling place county,” said Olivia Hale, San Joaquin County Registrar of Voters. “There is a box of preprinted ballots that are sealed that in the event they run out of ballots, they’re able to call our help desk, they give them permission to open those emergency ballots. Once those emergency ballots are open, then we’re deploying more paper immediately.”
 Q: How can a voter report a complaint, and what is the process for resolving it? 
 Voters can generally raise a concern with a poll worker or contact the county elections office. Counties said they would review the concern, resolve operational problems where possible and refer potential violations to the appropriate authorities.
 Every county identified a way to bring concerns to election staff or the elections office. Several also mentioned involving the Secretary of State’s Office or law enforcement.
 Solano County Registrar of Voters John Gardner encouraged anyone with a concern to notify a staff member to ensure there are witness accounts of the issue. Reports can be made after the fact through an online complaint form. 
 “We want to make sure our staff can document if it’s someone within the 100-foot limit that they really verify they’re in that 100-foot limit. They have the ability to deescalate some of those situations and could resolve a complaint right on the spot,” Gardner said.
 In San Joaquin County, there is a voter-feedback survey available. 
 “We evaluate any and all complaints and/or concerns regardless of political party,” said Nevada County Registrar of Voters Armando Salud-Ambriz. “If there is potential liability to any sort of voter fraud or violation we then send it over to respective law enforcement partners, sometimes the Secretary of State’s Office.”
 Elections officials can be contacted by phone or email. If on-site, officials encouraged voters to speak with the vote center manager.
 Q: What rules apply to voters who are in line when polls close? How are delayed openings documented, and can voting hours be extended? 
 Election Day runs from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. in California.
 Officials said anyone in line at 8 p.m. can still vote. Workers typically identify the last person in line so those who arrive afterward are not added.
 Sutter, Stanislaus, Solano and Sacramento explicitly described identifying or stationing someone at the end of the line when polls closed to ensure those already in line can still vote.
 Salud-Ambriz said in very specific situations, hours can be adjusted, but elections officials do not have the power to make those decisions unilaterally. 
 “There are legal options that we have. It mainly consists of a court order and/or judgment in support with the California Secretary of State’s Office,” he said. “The ability is there, but we can’t just say it.”
 While the following scenarios are uncommon, officials also responded to the following serious but less common situations.
 Q: What may poll watchers observe or challenge under state and local rules? Who is responsible for addressing a watcher who crosses the line? 
 Members of the public may observe election processes, and officials generally welcomed that oversight. Observers must follow the rules: they cannot intimidate voters, interfere with workers or compromise ballot privacy. If someone oversteps, workers may explain the rules, contact the elections office or involve law enforcement when necessary. Observers are not new to elections.
 “Every process is observable by the public -- and that includes any special interest groups,” said Ken Casparis, a spokesperson for Sacramento County. “We do have rules that they are expected to abide by. They cannot interfere in any way with any of the processes and that includes interfering with particular voters at vote centers who are trying to cast their ballot. We have rules for where they can and cannot observe.”
 Casparis said voters are entitled to privacy and that poll watchers may be subject to removal by vote center staff if they infringe on that privacy. Citizens are invited to observe processes, Casparis said. For example, that includes watching tabulation, watching staff pull ballots from envelopes, or monitoring signature verification.
 Rules explaining what poll watchers are and are not allowed to do are often posted.
 Q: What is the protocol for protecting voters and keeping voting locations open in the event of a disruption? 
 Poll workers would contact the elections office or, for a serious threat, law enforcement. Counties said they coordinate with local law enforcement before elections and would respond according to the situation, with the goal of protecting voters and keeping voting accessible. 
 Stanislaus County staffs a hotline for its election workers to call if a problem outside their scope of training arises, and added that its teams meet with law enforcement partners ahead of Election Day to ensure they are aware of the location of polling places and are briefed on any possible issues that may arise.
 Q: What access would federal officers or National Guard personnel have at a polling location, and under what circumstances might they be present? What should voters do if they are questioned by law enforcement or immigration officials? 
 Officials generally said that no one should intimidate voters or interfere with voting. 
 Salud-Ambriz, of Nevada County, advised voters to remain calm, avoid confrontation and notify election officials if a situation with a federal, state or other individual were to arise.
 Uniformed officers should generally not be at polling places, officials said, unless they are there to vote themselves or to respond to a specific call at the voting location. 
 “While our office doesn’t have authority over law enforcement agencies, we have procedures in place to respond to disruptions at Vote Centers. Anyone who feels threatened or believes their ability to vote is being interfered with should notify a Vote Center staff member immediately so we can respond appropriately,” Casparis said.
 Q: Who maintains custody of completed ballots, and how does custody transfer throughout the counting process and afterward? 
 Officials who addressed custody described ballots being secured at voting locations and transferred to election staff under documented procedures. 
 In Sutter County, ballots remain under the inspector’s custody; two people return them to the elections office for central scanning, Johnston said.
 In Stanislaus County, Linder said completed ballots remain with county-employed staff and are always accompanied by two employees; custody is tracked between locations and county facilities.
 Gardner, of Solano County, explained the process like this:
 “At our polling locations, ballots are deposited into a device that actually counts them at that moment,” he said. “There's a scanner that sits on top of a secured box. The paper ballot goes down into that box where it is secured all day long. At the end of the night, the poll workers will open that box and kind of seal the container that the paper ballots are in and from that point, the custody is maintained.”
 He said poll workers then hand the sealed box off to a certified transfer team. 
 “They sign a transfer form that says, I gave this box with this seal number to this team that comes to our office. And again, we sign that transfer form to verify the box was still sealed up and it goes into our secure facility.”
 Elections officials largely described excitement heading into Election Day and a commitment to making voting safe and accessible. Some reported strong early participation while others emphasized the work still to come in the days and weeks ahead.
 Q: What is the review or referral process if an election official alleges fraud during voting or counting? 
 The general response was that workers should raise concerns with the elections office, which can gather facts, address operational issues and refer potential violations for investigation. 
 Statewide voting contacts 
 Confidential voter hotline: 800-345-VOTE (8683) — for suspected election fraud, misconduct or violations of voting rights.
 Election Fraud Investigation Unit: 916-657-2166.
 The secretary of state also accepts an Election Voter Complaint Form
